subtopic: PAYMENT OF BANK OF CANADA NOTES
PAYMENT OF BANK OF CANADA NOTES
speechtext:
1.	As the Bank of Canada notes stipulate that the said bank will pay to the bearer, on demand, the amount printed on the said notes, at what offices of the Bank of Canada is it possible to obtain payment for the said notes?
2.	What does the Bank of Canada use to pay these promissory notes?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PAYMENT OF BANK OF CANADA NOTES
speechtext:
1 and 2. The unit of Canadian currency is "the dollar". Certain forms of currency, including Bank of Canada notes, have, by statute, been given the status of legal tender, and these are the legal means of discharging any obligation expressed in terms of Canadian dollars. Subsection 1 of section 25 of the Bank of Canada Act provides for redemption of Bank of Canada notes in gold bars, but under the authority of subsection 2 of this section this requirement has been suspended since March 11, 1935. Under present conditions, therefore, the phrase "will pay to bearer on demand" on a Bank of Canada note, which is in itself legal tender as mentioned
above, means that it is payable in legal tender of other denominations if required by the holder.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will give an oral answer to this question, although I doubt if it is a proper question. Questions are for the purpose of obtaining information on matters which relate to the responsibility of the government in its administration of the country's affairs. The government or any member of the government, cannot be expected to be obliged to answer questions which refer to arrangements made or understandings reached between members of an administration and any of their followers. I shall be very glad, however, to give my hon. friend such information as I am in a position to give at this moment. His question relates to so-called pledges or undertakings given by certain members of the Liberal party at the time of their appointment to the senate that they would, if the question of senate reform came up, support in the senate such legislation in that particular as the government of the day might wish to have enacted.
Perhaps I can make the circumstances clear by reminding my hon. friend that when the
Questions

Liberal administration came into office in 1921, and for some time thereafter, there were very few Liberals in the senate; there was a very strong opposition. Some of the measures which went from the House of Commons to the Senate wrere defeated there by the opposition; and our government at the time felt, as the British government did in 1911, that something in the nature of a parliamentary act might be necessary in order to ensure that our social and other classes of legislation would not be defeated indefinitely through opposition in the senate.
It was that kind of thing which was in my mind when I spoke with different gentlemen before they were formally appointed to the senate and received their assurance that, in situations of the kind, they would support legislation for senate reform that might come to the senate from this house.
There was nothing in the nature of a written pledge. There was no pledge made to the government, as a government. It was an undertaking that was given to myself, as the one who was responsible for nominating members to the senate. How many there were from whom I received that assurance, I cannot say at the present time. Nor am I in a position to say just when I ceased to raise that question. It did not become as important later on, when we had a majority in the Senate, and were in a position to see that permanent legislation originating in this house was not defeated because of action on the part of a hostile opposition in the upper chamber.
My bon. friend also asked:
What is the present membership of the senate; how many were appointed on the recommendation of Mr. Bennett; how many have been appointed on the recommendation of the present Prime Minister; how many were appointed on the recommendation of any other Prime Minister; how many support the government and how many are in the opposition.
My hon. friend will obtain that information from the same source from which I would be able to secure it, namely the Parliamentary Guide, which contains information respecting appointments to the senate. Indeed, from the point of view of some bon. gentlemen opposite, I might err in making a statement in answer to that part of his question, were I to attempt to give my own views as to the political complexion of some of the hon. members in the senate. When Sir Robert Borden was prime minister it will be recalled that for a time he was prime minister of a Conservative government and for a time of a coalition government. Some of us thought that the coalition government soon became the same
fMr. Mackenzie King.]
thing as a Conservative government; so I would not care to answer that question. My hon. friend will have to get his information from sources which are available; it is not one I could be expected to answer.
Then the hon. member asks further:
Has the practice of securing pledges with respect to Senate reform from prospective senators been discontinued? If so, at what date?
And the further question:
What Senate reforms have been implemented during the past twenty years and what was the nature and date of each such reform?
I have already answered the first of these questons.
The question as to what reforms have been made is a matter of public record. I might regard one thing as a reform, and the hon. member might regard something quite different as a reform. That is a matter of public record which he will have to work out for himself.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, February 3, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King that a select committee be appointed to examine and report on the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living and matters pertaining thereto.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, certain facts have emerged out of the debate which has taken place in this house during the past two days which the members of my party view with a great deal of gravity. We have felt from the outset that the setting up of a committee is not the kind of action which the country needs at the present time. We have felt that this committee will delay effective action on the part of the government in meeting the situation
which has arisen and which is continuing to grow worse from week to week and from month to month.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
Someone says, "Oh, no," but may I say that at three o'clock this afternoon the wires carried the new cost of living index for December. On December 1, 1947, the cost of living index stood at 146; on January 2, 1948, a month later, it had risen to 148-3. The increase in the month of December was 2-3 points. The higher prices for food that have been prevailing for a month are not reflected in the cost of living index which was issued this afternoon. I think this highlights the necessity for the government's taking effective action, not for the setting up of a committee.
Reference has been made to the price spreads committee of 1934. I looked up the record to see how long it took that committee to make its report. On February 2, 1934, just fourteen years ago to the very day that we began to discuss the resolution now before us, the order of reference for the setting up of the committee passed this house. On February 22, twenty days later, the first meeting was held. The last meeting was on June 22, 1934. Then, as hon. members will recall, the committee became the royal commission. On October 30, 1934, the royal commission met for the first time. On February 1, 1935, one year later, the last meeting of the commission was held, and on April 9, 1935, it reported. Confirmation of what I have said will be found in the report of the commission which I have before me.
The occasion for the appointment of the price spreads committee arose through certain charges made by a then minister of the crown, Hon. H. H. Stevens, regarding Canadian industry. Mr. Stevens, as a minister, having made charges, naturally set out to substantiate them. In other words, officers of the department and other officials available to the minister and the committee were definitely in the position of desiring to produce evidence and to confirm certain statements that had been made about the depressed price levels of 1934. The situation today is entirely different. The government now in office has allowed the cost of living to rise month by month until in the month of December last it increased by the phenomenal percentage of 2-3. Therefore the conditions surrounding the setting up of this committee are in that respect different from those which existed at the time of the appointment of the price spreads committee in 1934.
Prices Committee

Various members of the opposition sitting on this side of the house have endeavoured to enlarge the scope of the present committee and empower it to make recommendations, but such requests from this side of the house have been denied. True, the amendment and subamendment were ruled out of order, but I submit, Mr. Speaker, that we might not have been ruled out of order. The question of the validity of the amendment and of the subamendment would not have arisen had their validity not been challenged by the government. Consequently the opposition in this house has the right, I think, to feel angry at the situation at whidh we find ourselves, and the country has the right to feel as the opposition does, for the country is asking for bread in a very real sense, Mr. Speaker, and what .they are getting is a stone. They are asking for action, and they are getting a committee.
All the facts that this committee could, find Should now be in the possession of the government or departments of government. If further facts need to be established, all the machinery necessary to that end is available. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself stated in 1934 when the price spreads committee was under discussion that under the Combines Investigation Act all the power existed that was necessary, and the right hon. gentleman added that he knew that was so because he himself had been, if not wholly, at least largely responsible for the drafting of that act. Consequently we have there the machinery which should have been used ever since the price level began to rise, and it should be used now.
I do not think that the opposition in this house should be placed in the position of having to accept a committee which has no power to make recommendations, or one which is to exercise a function which should be fulfilled through the machinery of the Combines Investigation Act and the wartime prices and trade board. The government has all the power and assistance it requires now. This house in December last voted to extend the government's emergency powers until March 31, and I have no doubt that when the time comes the house will extend those powers until March 31, 1949, or until such time as those powers may no longer be required to protect the interests of the people. Why does not the government use the power it has? Why does it seek to set up a committee which will in all probability be used very largely to divert public attention from the real issue, the increase in the cost of living? I will not say it is done for that purpose, but

the government, I say, is shelving the responsibility which is properly that of the government, and, sir, I make this statement, that under the circumstances the members on the opposition side would' be quite justified in saying to the government: We are going to be no party to this manoeuvre; we have no desire to participate in a committee of this description. I think the opposition would be justified in saying that to the government at this time. I feel very strongly about this, because the people need the protection that the government is ndt giving.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent), in a speech made in this house the other evening, outlined what the government had done during the war to keep down prices and prevent inflationary price levels. He made a splendid defence of the use of the powers which this house granted to the government as late as last December. If that could be done on former occasions it could have been done ever since it became evident that the cost of living was on the increase to the degree to which it has risen. I have already mentioned that there was an increase of 2-3 in the cost of living in the month of December last. In the year between January 1, 1947, and January 1, 1948, the increase in the cost of living was 21-3 points.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
I had thought at first that I might try to improve the resolution of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) by way of amendment; but I am now convinced, seeing that others have made a concerted effort to broaden the scope of the present motion, that the chances would be remote that any amendment we might offer would be accepted. It is my opinion that the Prime Minister is quite determined that the resolution shall stand as it is. That, I think, is unfortunate for several reasons which I shall try to give as I go along.
I can only agree with many of the remarks that have already been made, and particularly the reference to action. I am quite convinced that the people of Canada are concerned about the rapid rise in the cost of living. The Prime Minister must be aware of that fact or he would not have seen fit to introduce the resolution now before us. But I believe the Prime Minister and the people are also aware that this tremendous rise in the cost of living is not something that has happened only recently. It is something that has existed for a period of years. The rise in the cost of living has been a continuing process now for a long period of time, and particularly since the end of the war.
Take agricultural products. I suggest that one thing that the people are concerned about is, not the fact that agricultural products have risen so high, but the fact that the people themselves have not enough purchasing power to buy those products at present costs. I maintain that prices of agricultural products are not in themselves too high when one considers the costs of production and the necessity of giving to the farmer a fair return on the commodities he produces. I am firmly convinced, however, that the money, the purchasing power, in the hands of the people does not enable them to purchase food commodities at present daily prices.
It is a fact, which has been drawn to my attention, particularly in my own city of Calgary, that a great number of people, a great number of veterans too, may I add, are finding it - impossible to live on $35 a week and raise a family. These people have come to me not singly but by the dozen complaining, and their complaint is that they cannot get along on the amount of money they receive. That is something which it does not 5849-55J
take a committee to investigate. The government itself has the machinery whereby it can ascertain the same thing at any time.
In the remarks that were made the other day a distinction was drawn between world conditions at the time the price spreads committee was set up and the conditions that prevail today. One of the ministers said that the situation was entirely different, that that was in a period of depression and falling prices. I would point out to the Prime Minister, however, that even at that time the people found themselves in the same difficulty that exists today, because in 1934 they were faced with exactly the same situation from the point of view of purchasing power. They did not have at that time the purchasing power to pay the prices that were being asked even then. The conditions which brought about the results might have been different, but the results were the same so far as the consuming public was concerned.
I think the Prime Minister would be well advised to rectify some of the things I am now pointing out, resulting from low purchasing power in the hands of the people. Take, for instance, old age pensions. I am sure the Prime Minister will agree with me that it does not take a committee of the house or a royal commission to come to the conclusion that the purchasing power in the hands of old age pensioners, on the basis of their pensions, is certainly not sufficient to buy food, clothing and shelter at present prices. It simply cannot be done, and we do not need a committee to investigate that.
Take veterans' allowances. The government knows what the situation is. Indeed, it has made provision for assisting veterans, especially those going to university; or, if it has not already done so, it is considering the question. There again, however, I point to the fact that the government has the machinery to investigate these cases as well. We do not need a committee for that purpose. I think one of the best ways to increase the purchasing power of the people in order to meet the tremendous costs, of which we are all cognizant, would be to increase the family allowance. At this moment I am not going to argue whether the way the money was raised in order to give family allowances the proper way. I think another way could have been found; but I think the underlying principle of a family allowance to supplement wages, salaries and commissions is entirely sound. The government could increase those allowances; as the last speaker pointed out, they have a tremendous surplus and that money could be used for that purpose. This action would not
Prices Committee

require any committee or commission,, but it would bring immediate results.
A great deal of attention has been devoted to the difference between the price spreads committee and the committee being set up under this motion. I wish to refer to that point again, even though some of what I have to say may be repetition. I have gone very carefully over all the speeches made in this house when the price spreads committee was set up in 1934, and it is my view that the committee was set up at that time to investigate the same sort of thing this new committee will be investigating. In fact at that time they went much farther in investigating causes than the present committee is being permitted to go, if it is set up at all. For instance, in 1934 the spread being investigated was between the wages the workers were receiving and the prices they had to pay for the goods when they were produced. There was a tendency toward lower wages. The cost of material entered into the question; the cost of financing entered into it; the cost of overhead entered into it. However, there was that difference, and at that time they merely referred to it as a price spread.
Under the present resolution we are undertaking an investigation into the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living. The costs are exactly the same. Those costs may be greater, as the resolution indicates, because some of these products have been withheld from the market, thereby forcing up the price. Cost factors will come into the picture; interest charges will come into the picture; yet it has been indicated by ministers of the crown that there is no intention of allowing this committee to investigate the financing of companies across this country. I maintain that you cannot find out the cost factors unless you go into all these matters. It has already been indicated by the government that labour conditions will not be investigated. The price spreads committee did investigate the labour factor in regard to the rise in costs. In any cost investigation, whether it be called the cost of living or the price spread, I do not think you can eliminate these necessary factors and say the committee shall not have power to go into them.
When I was reading over the speech of the present Prime Minister in reference to the setting up of the price spreads committee I noticed that he pointed out this very fact, suggesting to the then prime minister how important it was that the committee should look into the method employed by various companies in financing their operations. He pointed out that watered stock might be one cause; that floating large bond issues might be another

cause; that borrowing money at high rates of interest might be another. I have the volume of Hansard before me, with the page marked, but I need not bother reading it because it has already been put on record. Therefore, when one realizes that the work to be done by these two committees is so very similar, one wonders why the Prime Minister takes such objection to having the scope of the present committee enlarged so as to be able to do the work expected of it.
I now want to say a word about the power of the committee itself. The price spreads committee was given much greater power than the present committee. In my view it is wrong to tie the hands of a committee before it even starts work. I am to be a member of the committee, and I can foresee some of the difficulties that will be met. Both committees, it is true, were given power to send for persons, papers and records and of course that is absolutely necessary for any committee. But the price spreads committee had power to form a commission, if they considered it necessary, to investigate, for instance, labour problems. It was recognized in 1934 that a committee of this house could not possibly have the time to investigate all the cost factors that would arise as a result of labour conditions. I am sure the present committee would not have that time, either. Mr. Bennett, who was prime minister in 1934, went so far as to say he agreed that the committee would not have time at its disposal to make these separate investigations which in his view, as well as in the view at that time of the present Prime Minister, would be necessary to determine all the cost factors; so that the committee itself was given power to create commissions. I do not think it would be going too far to give the present committee power to set up a commission, if that were considered necessary. Of course I know the Prime Minister's reply to that. He will say, "Well, we have the Combines Investigation Act," and I intend to speak about that in a few moments.
Then, this committee is to have power to report its findings to the house. That was also true in 1934, but the present committee falls short in that it cannot make recommendation. The Prime Minister said he did not feel that this committee

I was going to say any committee, but that would not be right-should be asked to make recommendations. I disagree with that view. I believe the committee should make recommendations, and very strong recommendations, if it comes to a point where that is considered necessary. I was on the war expenditures committee, and I well recall that we came across matters which needed immediate attention. The committee made recom-

Prices Committee
mendations to the government, who took action immediately. It was not necessary to form a royal commission to investigate those matters. Some of those recommendations were even telephoned or wired back to the government, when the committee was meeting outside Ottawa. So that I believe this committee will be greatly handicapped if it has not power to make recommendations. Of course it can report. All committees report to the house from time to time, but it seems to me that when we take away the power of recommendation we are absolutely killing the effect of the committee.
When you compare the price spreads committee of 1934 and the prices committee of 1948 you find that the work involved is almost the same; that is, it is an investigation into the rise in costs. I do not care whether you call it a spread or a rise; it is the difference between what an article should be sold for and what it is being sold for. But while the work of both committees is the same, the hands of the present committee are tied to such an extent that it cannot begin to perform the sort of duty which was performed by the price spreads committee. I think it is wrong when you shackle the hands of a committee before it even gets started. Generally speaking, I would say that the scope of this resolution is entirely too narrow. For instance, the Prime Minister pointed out that it is factfinding committee. It is true that, at least to some extent every committee of the house is a fact-finding committee; otherwise it would not be appointed. Each committee investigates some condition or another, and the purpose of a committee is to find facts. Therefore that is nothing new when applied to any committee.
Then the Prime Minister referred to the function of the Combines Investigation Act. He pointed out to the late Viscount Bennett, when he was prime minister in 1934, that the Combines Investigation Act was sufficiently broad to take in- any and' all of the things which a committee set up at that- time was expected to take in. What the Prime Minister has said in that regard has, in part, been placed on the record orally. However, I believe I should go to the extent of placing on Hansard the exact words of the Prime Minister, so that there may be no suggestion of any attempt to alter the phrasedlogy used at that time.
May I point out that, in my view, the Prime Minister's statement of that day was sound, but for the life of me I cannot see why he now takes the opposite view. To my mind, the work of the committee of that day and of the one now proposed is identical, with
the exception that the earlier committee set up to investigate price spreads and mass buying was given a much wider scope in its methods of investigation than is the one now proposed.
As reported at page 191 of Hansard for February 2, 1934, the Prime Minister said:
There is one other aspect which I think is perhaps even more important. It is that the government has already legislation available to deal with matters of this kind, if it will view the whole question sympathetically.
And then, this important statement:
Legislation is one thing, but the administration of existing law is quite another.
I contend, holding the same view as the Prime Minister held at that time, that the legislation is there, and if the government wishes to take a sympathetic view it has the machinery right now to do everything it expects this committee to do. Then he went on to say:
I do not think one need go beyond what has taken place in the last three or four years to recognize very clearly that no matter what the laws may be, unless the department of the government that administers them is wholly sympathetic with the object in view, the law will serve very little purpose. We have on the statutes a Combines Investigation Act which provides all the machinery necessary for the purpose of making the fullest possible kind of inquiry into any matter preventing or lessening competition or restraining trade.
Cost factors do restrain trade, and they are mentioned in the resolution. Hoarding is in restraint of trade; that, too, is mentioned in the resolution. Then he goes on to say:
. . . effective machinery, machinery giving all the powers and affording as well all the safeguards needed in connection with inquiry into matters of this land.
Then, if that was not sufficient, the Prime Minister further emphasized the point by saying, as reported at page 192:
May I add that the Combines Investigation Act contains within its provisions ample powers for all the investigation that need be made to guide the government in the matter of further legislation? The legislation is already therq, we do not need to wait for a committee of this house to report on these matters. There _ is ample provision in the act for conducting inquiry if the government is really in earnest.
The Prime Minister should take that to heart. If the government is really in earnest, the machinery is there; the government knows the causes and should do something about the matter. Then he states further, in the next column:
The public are looking at this session not for further inquiry or further royal commissions, but for action in the nature of legislation.
Prices Committee

I do not think I could express that thought nearly as effectively as the Prime Minister did on that occasion. I believe, with the Prime Minister, that there is sufficient legislation and sufficient power in the hands of the government to make any inquiry and any law it desires to make, and to take any action it desires to take. I have pointed out some of the ways in which I believe the condition could be rectified immediately.
Some observations have been made concerning the formation of the committee. I can see both advantages and disadvantages in having a committee of this kind, and I have pointed out some of them. However, one thing of which we must be most careful is that we shall not have a delaying action. The government must do something now; and then, if it likes, let the committee proceed with its investigation, because it will take a long time for the committee to reach the point where it can make an intelligent report back to the house.
It has been said by some hon. members, and in particular by the leader of the C.C.F. party, that large profits are being made. I believe large profits have been made, and I agree with the hon. member in that respect, although I am not in a position to prove it. I can merely make that assertion, and I believe the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) expressed himself in a similar fashion. This committee would give a first-class opportunity to the Minister of Labour and the leader of the C.C.F. to bring their statements to light, not only for the information of parliament but for that of the people of Canada at large. I am sure it would have a great effect in the lowering of prices.
I do not believe, however, that the mere procedure of holding those people up as an example would be sufficient. If a concern dealing in that fashion is caught, it should be treated accordingly.

speechtext: Do the terms of reference allow for inquiry into profits?

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
No, they do not; and that is the very point to which I have been referring. I mentioned a while ago that the Prime Minister himself, speaking with respect to the price spreads and mass buying committee, took exception to the action taken by the late Viscount Bennett, by stating that there should be an extension of the powers of the committee then proposed, and suggesting that its powers should be extended to the point of examining into the financing of the companies involved. I believe that was necessary then, and that it is just as necessary today; because, if we are to find out whether or not there has been profiteering, we must

go into all aspects of the matter, and that will take time. If it should develop that the leader of the C.C.F. or the Minister of Labour can prove his charges, then appropriate action should be taken, and I urge that the powers of the committee be extended to give that opportunity.
The question of controls has been discussed. I cannot see why the committee should not have the power to recommend to the government the continuation of controls, if it thinks such action is necessary. I have always held the view that necessaiy controls should be retained, and that necessary subsidies should be applied. But controls, for the mere sake of controlling, will not get us anywhere or solve our problems. The same applies to subsidies. We have pointed out on many occasions where, in our view, the government has removed subsidies too rapidly.
May I refer more specifically to the resolution? The leader of the Social Credit party (Mr. Low) pointed out the other day that there were certain changes which he thought should be made. He stated that at the appropriate time we would offer amendments, but it is quite evident that it would be a useless waste of the time of the House of Commons to move any amendment to this resolution. We considered them worthwhile. There were some things which the leader of this party thought should be done.
One was that the word "recent" should be deleted from the resolution. I think that word was put in intentionally; in fact the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) said that it was. The first paragraph of the resolution reads:
(a) the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living.
As soon as I read that, I wondered why the word "recent" was there. Everyone knows that the causes of the rise in tie cost of living are not a recent thing; they have -been in existence for some length of time. When the minister was speaking the other day on that section he said, as reported on page 773 of Hansard of February 2, 1948:
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) suggests that the word "recent" should not be there. I can tell the hon. member that it was n-ot there in the first drafts that we had prepared. But you had to have some point from which -the rise started, and it was felt that it would be dangerous and hampering to insert any date, that it might well be left to the committee to determine what the public was concerned about, and that the time factor might very well vary according to the results of the investigation after it got under way. It was felt that a committee of this house could be trusted to construe that in a reasonable way to achieve for the Canadian- public what it would feel the Canadian public wished to know.

Prices Committee
It was no accident that the word "recent" was put in there. The minister said that it was necessary to have a time limit. It is quite evident that the government has in mind that the committee shall go back only so far, because the minister says that there must be a time limit. I can quite see why they did not want to put in a date because, if they had, they would be saying in effect that that was the deadline, that that was as far as the committee would dare go, that they could not go one hour beyond that. The majority of the committee being Liberal members, the government knows just how the word "recent" will be interpreted. There is no question about that. Just consider the contradictions in the minister's statement. He first said that there must be a deadline, and then he went on to say:
It was felt that a committee of this house co-uld be trusted to construe that in a reasonable way to achieve for the Canadian public what it would feel the Canadian public wished ito know.
If the committee could be trusted, why put a gun at its head and say, "Yes, we will trust you, but be careful what you do." That is exactly what the government do there. Not only are there restrictions as to the scope of the investigation; there is a time limit as well. The committee is to deal with only recent rises. Such an expression is ridiculous, and it ill becomes the Secretary of State for External Affairs to make such a statement to this house. It is just insulting the intelligence of hon. members when he says, on the one hand, that we must have a deadline and then, on the other, that surely we can trust the committee.
We thought, and we think yet, that the word "recent" should be struck out of the resolution. There is nothing in the resolution that so hinders the work. If this committee ever gets started to work, one of the things it will have to deal with is the causes of the rise in the cost of living, and if it is to investigate those causes, one of the things it will have to take into consideration is taxes. I think every hon. member on this side of the house and, I venture to say, a great many on the other side, have it in mind that one of the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living is the hidden nuisance taxes. The Secretary of State for External Affairs tried to ridicule that idea, and he mentioned liquor as an example. I think his example was ill chosen, because there is not a member in this house who does not agree with the minister in regard to that commodity. If people want to spend their money foolishly on liquor, then they should pay the taxes imposed on
liquor, but to compare the hidden taxes on liquor with the hidden taxes on the cost of living is a ridiculous thing to do. There is just no comparison at all. The minister quoted figures as to these hidden taxes but he did not give the whole picture by about S700 million. Perhaps he thinks that is close enough.
Another thing that I mentioned a while ago was the question of subsidies. If this committee ever goes to work, and I say that advisedly, it might find that same of the. costs are legitimate. For instance, it might find that the price of butter is legitimate, due to all the cost factors entering into its production. I am sure that the committee would find also that the purchasing power of the people is such that it does not permit them to buy butter at those prices. What are you going to do? I think the committee should be in a position to be able to suggest to the government and to this house what should be done. If the committee thinks subsidies provide a remedy, then the committee should have the power to make that recommendation. During the war we found that condition to be true. The government saw fit to pay subsidies after a great deal of persuasion, and they worked in keeping down the cost of living. If they worked, then there is no reason why they should not work now if they are handled judiciously and properly.
May I suggest that when you set up a committee of this type you must give it a broad field to investigate, and that will take a lot of time. My judgment is that one of the things causing an increase in prices is the trade agreements which we have entered into. My mind goes back to a year or so ago when we entered into agreements under Bretton Woods and Dumbarton Oaks. In passing, may I say that both the Conservative and C.C.F. parties agreed that the policy which the government was following then was the right one. By their agreeing they gave the government the green light to go ahead and put through the agreements, and I think it ill becomes those parties to criticize the government now for the action they took, especially when that action resulted in increased costs of living to our people.
One of the direct results of those trade agreements was the embargo placed on certain British goods coming into this country, and another direct result was the twenty-five per cent excise tax which added to the cost of living. Is that not a cost factor? Some of those who are complaining about the rise in costs are partly to blame for it and they must take their share of the responsibility.
Prices Committee

That is a matter which this committee should be permitted to investigate if it is to investigate the rise in the cost of living.
I have pointed) out the objections I have to this committee. Some advantages may come from its work, but there are a great many things to hamper its work. As a member of 'the committee I do not want to take part in any committee which will not be in a position to bring back to the house a decent, honest and constructive report. On every committee on which I have sat I have always done the best I could. I want to be in a position to do the same on this committee, and I am sure that the other members of the committee feel as I do.
I was much concerned the other day to hear one of the members of the committee who sits on the other side of the house objecting to the amendments that have been put forward to broaden the scope of the committee. He himself was one of the nine Liberal members who will constitute a majority on that committee, as against the seven other members, and naturally, therefore, the Liberal members on the committee will be in a position to interpret the word "recent" in such a way as to hamper the effectiveness of the committee's work. I would have thought he would have been willing to give the committee the largest possible scope so that it would be in a position to bring back to the house the most useful report it possibly could. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that that will be the aim of this group, to bring back data which will be of a constructive nature. We have always endeavoured to take that stand. That is the stand we took on the removal of subsidies and on the Bretton Woods agreement, and we do not happen to have been wrong on that occasion, as later events proved.
I should like to see the government do something immediately about the cost of living, to increase the purchasing power of the people so that they can meet these increased costs. Then, if the government wants to go on and have an investigation, it should be undertaken with the sincere and earnest desire to get the best results possible.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that every member of this house was moved by the declaration made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) when he introduced the resolution and asked, as reported at page 751 of Hansard, that all members of the house for the time being forget their party politics and do their utmost in connection with the investigation of this urgent and important problem. But then when we on this side of the house endeavoured to co-

operate by giving the committee the powers it should have to make recommendations, in order that we might make our contribution effective and do something constructive to meet the problem, the committee was hobbled by the narrow scope of the motion and denied the opportunity of getting down to essentials.
I cannot understand that attitude on the part of the Prime Minister. When the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) moved an amendment which would enlarge the scope of the committee and bring it into line with the powers of other committees in the past, the attitude taken by the government was:	No;
you shall be hobbled; you shall be restrained; you shall make no recommendations whatsoever. The same attitude was taken by the government when the leader of the C.C.F. party moved a subamendment. Finally when the leader of the Social Credit party pointed out that the word "recent" in the terms of reference would deny any investigation beyond the immediate present, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) said he would not accept that.
A non-political committee? A committee uncontrolled by the government? One of the ministers is chairman of the committee and four of the parliamentary assistants are members of it. I say to you, sir, that if the Prime Minister had intended to remove political considerations from this problem he would have had a committee set up which would have been equally representative of all parties in the house. He would not have proposed a committee which in the ordinary run of things would be dominated in whole or in part by the cabinet.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO INQUIRE INTO PRICE INCREASES AND MATTERS PERTAINING THERETO
speechtext:
The committee is set up by the government. Its minister of external affairs admits that the cost of living is a problem, but how it came about, he naively said, he did not know, and for that reason he found it necessary to speak to the house, not as a minister of the crown responsible to the people, but in the capacity of a common citizen of Canada. Sir, was there ever an admission made by a minister of the crown which was more condemnatory of the incompetence of the government he supports than the admission of the minister the other night? Here we are, he says, but we do not know how we got here; we do not know how we are going to get back, and as a common citizen, says the minister,
I would like the house to give me a few ideas, not how to get back to where wTe should be, but how we got where we are at the present time.

Prices Committee
I ask the Prime 'Minister when he replies to tell this house and the country why he denies to the members of the committee the right to make recommendations. I should have thought he would welcome recommendations. During the past few days some of his ministers have spoken. While the problem has been mounting and accelerating they have been travelling and making speeches. In every case where a committee has been set up by parliament to investigate prices such committee has been given the power to make recommendations. As was mentioned by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston), a committee on price spreads was set up in 1934. That committee was given certain powers-I will read the exact words:
That the committee shall report to the house from time to time its findings, together with recommendations of such measures as in the opinion of the committee may be considered necessary to secure as far as possible fair and just practices in the distribution and marketing systems of Canada, with fair and just returns to producers, employees, and employers, not inconsistent with the rights of consumers.
The motion instructed the members of that committee to make recommendations. As was pointed out by the preceding speaker (Mr. Johnston), the Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, said words to the effect that the committee was not needed. His conscience must have been bothering him, because when he made his opening speech on the motion it consisted of confession and avoidance in anticipation of criticism. The Prime Minister, on the motion now before us, said words to this effect; I know somebody will find out what I said in 1934; so he went into a lengthy disquisition, which would have done honour to a schoolman of the middle ages, in order to show the difference between conditions today and those in 1934. This is what he said in part in 1934, as reported at page 191 of Hansard of that year:
We have on the statutes a Combines Investigation- Act which provides all the machinery necessary for the purpose of making the fullest possible kind of inquiry into any matter preventing or lessening competition- or restraining trade.
I point out, too, sir, that also covers storage and hoarding. The Prime Minister went on and said: "What is really needed is sympathetic administration." Well, as I remember his speech on the night that his party came into power in 1935 if there was one thing more than another he was sympathetic to it was to the prosecution of monopoly privilege in this country. "A sympathetic administration"! Well, I should think that this government has had a sympathetic administration 5849-56
during the last few years. The Secretary of State for External Affairs formerly administered this act. Frankly the other night he did not know whether there was any evidence of exploitation1; he did not know whether anything had been done. He spoke as a common citizen of Canada. I wonder, sir, whether he did not speak as heir apparent?
Flying a kite.

I imagine, sir, what he would have said if he were on this side of the house and a committee were being set up with the power to be powerless. It is set up for the purpose of postponing action. The government is endeavouring by a subterfuge to get away from its responsibility of doing some-tiling, of having failed to do something in recent months. What the government is trying to do by this action is to smear somebody, to find a goat in order to get rid of its responsibility for failure to act.
I go back to 1919, and I may have an opportunity later to read some further statements made by the Prime Minister at that time. A committee was set up in 1919 to study the high cost of living. It was empowered to report to the house from time to time the results of its inquiry, with any recommendations the committee might wish to make with a view to effecting a reduction in prices and in rentals. Why does the Prime Minister not give this committee the legislative power that parliament can give to it, the power to act, if he wants action?
As I said a moment ago, the ministers do not know where they are going. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley) has not spoken yet. He presides over and is responsible under law for the administration of the Combines Investigation Act. Why does not he come in? Once it was said: "Speak of somebody and he is sure to appear". He is here now. I want him to tell the house and the country what has been done regarding the question of the high cost of living, what evidence the government has gathered together, what evidence the wartime prices and trade board is in a position to give, why during recent months there has in fact been little or no action taken by the board or the commissioner and his staff in connection with the Combines Investigation Act?
When the Prime Minister spoke the other day, in effect he said: What the government is going to achieve by this committee is this: by publicity we are going to frighten prospective wrongdoers. When Canada asked for action the Prime Minister gave them a discussion on morals. He said that if we went ahead under the Combines Investigation Act there would be obstacles in the way. That was an inter-
Prices Committee

esting statement. I quote from his remarks as reported at page 747 of Hansard:
There is a body of legislation already on the statute books of this country; but, as everyone knows, the minute an effort is made to set in motion some of this machinery, obstacles are raised from one side or another which tend to operate against speedjr and thorough action.
What are the obstacles? They are not on this side. What are the obstacles? Are there not the same obstacles in the way of the administration of this act as there were in instituting a prosecution against the dental corporations, when the people are questioning the prices of food and clothing? The Prime Minister continued;
Nothing will remove those obstacles so quickly as the power of a committee of this House of Commons to take up questions which affect the well-being of the people, something which adversely affects their lives.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Power of a committee which has no power.

These people who are profiteers-and if there be such they should be prosecuted-cannot be prosecuted, says the Prime Minister in effect, under the legislation which the Secretary of State for External Affairs two years ago said put real teeth in the act, not false teeth. The Prime Minister says there are obstacles in the way. I ask the Minister of Justice, were there any applications in the last year for the investigation of combines? What reports has the commissioner made to the minister as required by law? Has the Minister of Justice himself directed any inquiry against wrongdoers? These powers are given under that act. Have the provisions of the Inquiries Act been used? Two years ago the Secretary of State for External Affairs said; Give us the power and we will act. Two nights ago the minister said: I speak as a common citizen; I do not know whether anything can be done or has been done, and in common with other citizens of this dominion I should like to know whether anything can be done. It would be ludicrous if it were not so serious!
I ask the Minister of Justice, have any proceedings been taken, either in public or in private?-because under the Combines Investigation Act the commissioner has that power; or under the wartime prices and trade board whose administrator has the widest powers that anyone could have. At the risk of reiteration I am going to mention the powers the board is given and ask the Minister of Justice why, if there has been wrongdoing, have not these powers been used:
The board shall have power
(a) to investigate of its own motion or on complaint, costs, prices, profits and stocks of

goods and materials of any person engaged in the manufacture, importation, exportation, production, storage, transportation, supply or sale,
And so on. It covers everything that this committee is to be empowered to investigate, the only difference being that the commissioner can do something, whereas the committee can do nothing but report.
I ask the Minister o<f Justice, what has he done about section 8 '(1):
No person shall sell or offer for sale or supply any goods or services at a price that is higher than is reasonable and just, or withhold any goods or services from sale or supply for a price that is higher than is reasonable and just.
What has been done with that? The government had the machinery, said the Prime Minister in 1934. The only machinery that existed in 1934 was the machinery under t'he Combines Investigation Act. There is now additional machinery provided under the wartime prices and trade board, powers which were extended, as a result of the wishes of the government, until March 31 of this year.
The latest solution the Prime Minister offers is to call a committee of parliament together to sit and talk. They will sit and sift the evidence, and they might even shift the responsibility. When this committee starts to sit and to sift, how fearful the exploiters are going to be! I ask the Minister of Justice: Have you not been doing that ever since September? I have before me the Toronto Star of September 19. It is very close to sources that are close to the government. We can accept this. Here is what it said on that day:
Government rearguard action-
1 wonder what kind of action you call setting up a committee without power?
Government rearguard action against undue price increases in the wake of decontrol is being launched here through the wartime prices and trade board, and the combines investigation commission, official sources disclosed today.
What have they been doing in that regard? We have not heard the answer yet. We have heard from the heir apparent, and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner)-may I say that we from Saskatchewan know he has never lost a convention. If I may read further from the newspaper. The policy was this:
The program is designed to "scare" business against unjustified price boosts by two methods: threat of investigation and exposure where a combine in restraint of trade as suspected, and the release of information to the public indicating just what price increases are justifiable.
Apparently the minister of external affairs has not got beyond September, because that is the same policy that he and the Prime Minister believe is going to work now-to scare by

Prices Committee
publicity. I ask the government:	How has
the policy worked out? How often have they used it? They seem to have the most widespread opportunity for publicity. When have they named wrongdoers? When have they scared those who exploit? Yet today they say that a committee of parliament will do that what they have been trying to do ever since September last-with what success?
Does the government know what to do? The Prime Minister says there are obstacles in the way, so the law cannot well be used. What are the obstacles? I thought all the obstacles had disappeared on election night in 1935. The minister of external affairs-I always have difficulty in following him in the game of musical chairs-made a speech in AVinnipeg, and this is his policy:
We do not wish to be vengeful in such prosecutions as may be instituted but we do wish Canadians to realize provisions in the wartime price and trade board regulations are still the law.
That was his policy. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) came along last night, and I always like to hear him, because he is a breath of fresh air, no matter how trying he is to the government. He spoke too and announced the government's policy. Speaking in Quebec, he said:
The government intends to deal with them-
That is, the wrongdoers.
-as they should be dealt with. We must deal severely "with the greedy ones, no matter who they* are.
The minister of external affairs said we must not deal harshly with them, that all we want to do is to tell them about the wartime prices and trade board regulations. But the labour minister said we must deal severely with them. He continued:
It is this class which, more than anything else, threatens the future of the free enterprise system in Canada and in other parts of the world.
Then he announced the government's policy. There were different things we should do, but he believed there should be launched an educational campaign on the benefits of our way of life. One says, scare them by doing nothing; the other says, tell them what the law is; the third says, educate our people on Canada's way of life.
Then finally the Minister of Agriculture made a speech in Calgary. AVhat did he say? He was asked a question by the chairman of the Alberta wheat pool, whether the government was planning ceilings on wages and manufactured goods also. This was just January 19. And what was his answer? The answer was: "You would need the whole government 5849-561
to answer that". Then somebody said: "Would it help any if we went down there?" The answer was, "It might".
Here we are in the midst of the most difficult period in our history and the government sets up a committee. It asks parliament to set up a facsimile of power, a committee that will be powerless to act, a committee that will be gagged, its course predetermined.
Last night we had the sorriest picture of all, with a member of the committee saying that by amendment the house cannot add to the powers of the committee. We wanted an opportunity to go into these matters, to make a contribution, but the government says, "No. The committee shall be what we give you"- and it is a committee the like of which has never been set up in this country, with no power to bring in any recommendations. All it can do is sit and listen to evidence; and after it does that the Prime Minister says the government will know what to do. Mr. Speaker, Canada is entitled to know what has been done.
My hon. leader said something should be done about removing the sales tax. AVhat answer did he get from the Secretary of State for External Affairs? He did not deal with such things as food and clothing and the other things the ordinary man asks about today. He endeavoured to answer the argument by talking about liquor and cigarettes. Do those who suffer today because of high prices deserve to be treated with ridicule when they ask for relief? Again I go back to 1919. I have not time today to read anything more, but I have read some of the addresses of the then leader of the opposition, and I will refer to the dates so that those who wish may read his words for themselves. At that time, when the sales tax was one per cent, the then leader of the opposition, now the Prime Minister, pointed out how unfair it was. In 1921 he promised to remove the one per cent. In 1935 when, as I remember it, the sales tax was lower than today, he promised on election night that taxes of that kind, which rested upon the poof, would be removed. In 1920 he spoke on June 1, with his great knowledge of economics, of the unfairness of loading burdens on the backs of the poor. Now the Secretary of State for External Affairs comes along and ridicules the leader of the opposition when he suggests that if the government wants to attack this problem the first thing it should do is remove the sales tax from the things the people need in this country.
As the Prime Minister pointed out in that speech in 1920, the sales tax tends to pyramid over and over. The government stands to benefit by inflation, because the higher prices go
Prices Committee

the higher is the amount collected in sales tax. If prices before the war were 100 and now they are 200, on the original price the government is getting 20 per cent through this tax, due to the fact that the valuation has doubled during the period in question. Surely we in this parliament have a right to a declaration on this. If the government means what it says, that it wants to help the poor, that it wants to remove this load from the pensioner, the man of small income, why does the government not act when it pridefully speaks about its tremendous
While we talk about reducing taxes and reducing the cost of living, last November the government imposed another tax; and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) quite frankly admitted that the 25 per cent excise tax which was imposed upon many necessities was designed to put the price so high the Canadian people could not buy them. What is the government policy? Where do they stand? What do they intend to do?
Speaking of imposing taxes by order in council, I go back to October 14, 1935, election night, when the Prime Minister made a speech in which he said one of the reasons Mr. Bennett was defeated was that he was raising the bogey of communism. He went on to say of the election:
It constitutes a demand for the abolition of the extravagant increases in the tariff . . .
And today the tariff is higher than ever before in the history of this country.
. . . together with the removal of arbitrary taxes and regulations, as imposed by the present administration . . .
A promise to remove the sales tax was made thirteen long years ago. Then what a ring this next quotation has:
It is a demand for an end to the making and altering of tariffs by executive action-
Then he went on:
-and for the substitution of stability for uncertainty in the administration of customs laws.
What would he have said, in the face of that Hampdenesque declaration in 1935 if we, in power, had imposed taxation without the authority of parliament, something that had never been done in the history of our country or, indeed, the history of the British empire? Then he also said the election-
*-is a demand for the restoration of responsible government in Canada . . . I
I am not going to deal with that question ;oday.
It is a verdict in favour of personal liberty, electoral reform . . .
Speaking about tariffs and orders in council -and they are mentioned here, too-what a

situation we have when a minister rises in his place and says in effect that the promise made in 1941, 1942 and 1943 that compulsory savings would be returned to the people now is to be denied, not by act of parliament but by order in council passed in January. And, Mr. Speaker, there are many other matters to which I am not going to make reference on this occasion; but it is a great speech.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Hear, hear.
There is one who applauds.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: A great speech.

Yes, it is a great speech; but why have the promises made therein not been carried into effect? I say to the Prime Minister: to reduce the cost of living, first and foremost reduce the wasteful cost of government in this country. Deal with the question of the sales tax. Give to the Canadian people a lead, not the promise of a committee, rendered impotent, powerless, and emasculated in advance. Set up a committee representative of members of this house. Take parliament into your confidence; widen the scope of its powers; make it effective.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) asked the removal of the word "recent" in the resolution. It was no accident that the word "recent" was in the resolution. The Secretary of State for External Affairs said it was put in for a reason. The reason it was put in was to take from the shoulders of the government the responsibility the people of Canada know rests upon it because of its failure to act. In the course of his speech the Prime Minister said that what parliament wants and what the Canadian people want at this time is action. I have not his exact words before me at the present time, but I recall that that was the sense of what he said. We on this side, all members of the opposition, are united in one thing:	We want action. All
we have received from the government is a commitee that can postpone and procrastinate, thereby placing the government in a position of being able to say that until the committee reports, it cannot act. Above all, it denies members of this parliament the right to discuss the cost of living, rising prices and the like, in this chamber while the committee is sitting.
No.

Somebody says no. I ask the hon. member who interrupted to tell me who is Speaker of the house. Is it the Prime Minister? Your Honour is never subject to any direction. The Prime Minister

Prices Committee
read an opinion yesterday. My recollection is that on a number of occasions Your Honour denied us the right to information in the house regarding War Assets Corporation owing to the fact that a committee was sitting. You could not reverse yourself, sir, even with the opinion of the Prime Minister to the contrary. I say, sir, that we want to help, but we do not want to be fooled. We want action and are prepared to act. No one who has spoken for the government has shown in any way that they have tried to act. They have had the power; they have had the challenge; they have had the opportunity; but not one of them has been able to say that he, or the collective group sitting in the cabinet, has done anything to protect the Canadian people against what is generally admitted to be an unjustifiable increase in the cost of living.

I should like to give a ruling on the amendment presented by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Cold-well). It was moved by the hon. member, and seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis):
That all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor :
"this house is of the opinion that the present crisis demands and the people of Canada want not a parliamentary committee, but action by the government to restore price controls and subsidies."

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Would your Honour permit me to speak to the matter before you give your ruling?
No.
I wonder on what the hon. member could speak. I am giving my ruling.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: But, Mr. Speaker, after you give your ruling you do not permit hon. members to speak. The only opportunity we have to speak on the point of order is before you actually give your ruling. I am prepared to do so now, or after Your Honour has quoted any citations you may read provided that Your Honour permits me to speak before you actually give your ruling.

The hon. member knows that a Speakers ruling is not debatable. If he wishes to speak on the motion, it would be his privilege to speak.
Mr. KNOWLES1: I do not wish to speak to the motion now. But it is clear that you are about to make a ruling on the point of order raised by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken). You have quoted the rule correctly, that the Speaker's ruling is not debatable. So that if you give your ruling
we cannot say anything. Therefore I am asking permission now to speak to the point of order as to whether this motion is valid.
There is no point of order before the house. I do not believe any hon. member rose to a point of order on the amendment before the house.

The leader of the
opposition earlier this afternoon rose on a point of order. I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is quite in order when he asks permission to make comment upon it, before Your Honour rules.

I must call the attention of the hon. member to the fact that I was in the Chair when the leader of the opposition spoke about the amendment. He raised a point of order and called my attention to the fact that if it was my intention to decide that the amendment was out of order I should1 do so as soon as possible. That is what I understood. If the leader of the opposition rose to a point of order, stating that the amendment was out of order, I think it was at that time the hon. member should have spoken on the point of order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: He did not say it was out of order. He asked Your Honour to consider whether or not it was in order, and Your Honour gave no opportunity then for anyone else to speak. You said you would consider the matter and report later. If Your Honour is now going to rule it in order, that is fine; there is nothing else to say. But if you are going to give a citation indicating that, in your view, it is out of order, and then permit no one to answer, your ruling which follows will not be debatable.

The hon. member knows perfectly well the practice that when an amendment is put before the house it is the privilege of any hon. members to rise on a point of order and to discuss whether it is or is not. Then, when that has been done, it is the duty of the Speaker to decide if it is, or if it is not. I did not make the rules; the rules were made by the house and accepted by the house-just as they were accepted by the British House of Commons-that after a Speaker has given his ruling it is not debatable. I wonder how the hon. member can speak before I give my ruling.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It seems to me that the only way I can get at this is to rise to a point of order myself. I rise to a point of order.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
You cannot.

speechtext: I question the propriety of the course followed by the leader of the opposition in merely asking a question, rather than raising a specific objection to the motion before the house.

Order. I believe the hon. member will agree that a member should not rise on a point of order to discuss the attitude of a member respecting an incident which happened a few hours ago. If the hon. member had any point of order respecting the intervention of the leader of the opposition, he should have made it after the leader of the opposition had spoken.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Would you permit one further question?
Order. The hon. member will admit that-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-
Order. The hon. member will admit that I have discussed the matter already too much with him, and that it is not the practice for a Speaker to debate with any member of the house.

Mr. SPEAKER put the question as follows:
The motion before the house rvas moved bv Mr. King:
That a select committee of this house be appointed to examine and report from time to time as to:
(a)	the causes of the recent rise in the cost of living;
(b)	prices which have been raised above levels justified by increased costs;
(c)	rises in prices due to the acquiring, accumulating or withholding from sale by any persons, firms or corporations of any goods beyond amounts reasonably required for the ordinary purposes of their businesses.
Mr. Coldwell moved an amendment, seconded by Mr. Maclnnis:
That all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion that the present crisis demands and the people of Canada want not a parliamentary committee, but action by the government to restore price controls and subsidies."
I declared that amendment out of order. It is a well known principle, as expressed in 335 of Beauchesne's, third edition, that a motion may be amended: (a) by leaving out certain words; (b) by leaving out certain words in order to insert other words; (c) by inserting or adding other words. Please note that this well known rule does not authorize the striking out of all the words of a motion, it mentions only certain words.
The proposed amendment provides that the whole motion be struck out and that a new question be substituted for it. There is such a difference between the main motion and the hon. member's amendment that the latter cannot be considered as an amendment of the former. I consider that what he now proposes is an expanded negative, and moreover it further offends by the proposing of a declaration of opinion which should be .moved as a separate motion after notice. For these reasons I declared the amendment out of order and Mr. Knowles appeals from my decision.

I know that ministers of the crown have their departmental duties to attend to. Many of them have been switched around to other portfolios and, no doubt, are busying themselves getting a grip on the problems they have to face, and we hardly expect them to pay very much attention to the trend of the debates from day to day.
Many private members, have, of course, constituency problems and grievances that they want to air, but I suppose many of them are waiting until we resume the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. In the meantime many thousands of people are suffering beyond all bearing and are wondering when the government is going to get down to business and do something to check the rise in the cost of living, to reimpose controls and subsidies that are necessary, and to roll prices back to a reasonable level.
It is an amazing thing to me that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the ministers who surround him are so indifferent and so uncertain in their attitudes and can think of nothing more efficient in this serious situation than to suggest the creation of a parliamentary committee. Surely the government does not seek to imply that there is anything of a mystery about the present situation, a mystery that would call for the setting up of a committee of investigation. '
We of the C.C.P. group in the House of Commons have warned the government consistently, both in our speeches and in our amendments, and we have sought to focus the attention of the government upon what was bound to happen and what, unfortunately for a great many people concerned, has happened but the government would not listen to us. Oh, no, they listened to our Conservative friends to the right who demanded the immediate abolition of controls. They not only listened; they even went farther; they acted upon that very [DOT] unwise advice and hastily decontrolled, with the inevitable result that we have today a cost of living which the people cannot possibly face.
Today the government is on the spot, and the responsibility for the present mess rests squarely upon the government. I am satisfied that the government is not feeling very happy about it, but is trying to move over that responsibility to the tender mercies of a committee. It was the government and the government alone that introduced the stabilization policy that worked so well during the war years, and I believe that no one should deny to the government the credit

that is due for that policy. Just so long as wartime controls were in effect, prices were satisfactory to the people at large, and as far as I know there has been no demand from the consuming public to have these controls abolished. On the contrary, now that they have been abolished with such disastrous effect, there is a widespread and insistent demand that they be reimposed; and I believe, sir, that this demand should cause the government to give serious consideration to a review of its past actions. '
It is clear to me that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and his corps of experts knew very well what the situation would be on the withdrawal of the subsidies and controls, and for the information of the house I should like to quote from a brief statement culled from the columns of the Canadian Forum of December, 1947, which reads as follows:
Those who are inclined to feel that perhaps the government should not be held entirely responsible for the rise in prices, and that economic forces were too much for them, should read a recent speech of Mr. Abbott's in Toronto. The Minister of Finance stated categorically that prices have moved upward almost exactly as his experts forecast them at each step of decontrol and withdrawal of subsidies. That is an admission worth remembering, for the electors will know now where to put the blame. And of course that is where it belongs, with Mr. Abbott and his colleagues. We always knew that these appeals to business to behave were not meant seriously.
If there is a lingering doubt in the mind of the government as to what the people of Canada really want, and what is the real effect of the decontrol program, what is now taking place in western Canada should remove that doubt completely. A serious coal strike is now and has been in progress for some weeks in Alberta and in the Crowsnest Pass, part of which I have the honour to represent, and in the coal mining areas of Vancouver island. This strike has come about solely by reason of the rapid and unjustifiable rise in the cost of living, and of the inadequacy of their wages to meet it. I want to remind the house that our coal miners, the men who go down into the bowels of the earth to produce the precious coal which warms our homes and keeps the wheels of industry turning, cannot produce coal on a diet of sandwiches. They require heavy meals-meat, bacon, eggs, butter, cheese and the like-and I say again that for the purchasing of these items their wages are entirely inadequate. Here, then, in the depth of winter, when the need for coal is at its greatest, and when we have a serious threat of a fuel oil shortage, we find the production of coal in these large coal producing areas entirely at a standstill, and all that the govern-
