ment does about the matter is to talk about setting up a committee to see whether there has been any profiteering.
History tells us that Nero fiddled while Rome burned. I should like to say that that gentleman had nothing on this government. They merely dally with a grievous situation from day to day and week to week while people are being fleeced.
You will notice, Mr. Speaker, that I am not quoting many figures to prove what I am saying. It is not necessary that I should do so. Enough figures have been quoted in this house to prove that food prices are away out of line with wages. Figures have been given to prove that to any reasonable mind. Rather, I want to voice the national resentment against the removal of those beneficial controls that served the people of Canada so well during the war years; and here I want to point out to the government that, great as-was their responsibility to protect the persons of the citizens of this dominion from the dangers and terrors of war, it is no less their duty to protect the living standards of the people in times of peace.
As a member of this house, I am asking the government to act immediately to reimpose price controls and to pay subsidies where necessary; and while I am doing this I am thinking more particularly of those persons in the low-income groups, our old age pensioners, the recipients of social services allowances, our disability pensioners, the widows and dependents of veterans, and. last but not least, our veteran students. How these classes manage to exist on thpir meagre incomes is entirely beyond me. Their welfare is, I am sure, on the heart and mind of most of the members of this house, and it should be on the heart and mind of those who comprise the government.
The leader of this group, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), has spoken over the radio and also in this house calling the attention of the Prime Minister to the fact that there are three federal constituencies now vacant, and he has asked the government to name the dates for the election of members to this house so that the people in these constituencies may be represented. So far, that advice has not been taken. It may be, of course, that the government is not so sure that it has the full and complete confidence of the people. Be that as it may, these people are without representation; I would
urge the government to give serious consideration to the calling of elections in these constituencies; and especially as a member from British Columbia, I appeal on behalf of the constituents in Yale constituency. They should be represented in this house, and I hope that the government will give serious consideration to the calling of these elections. By doing so, the government would not only find out very speedily what it is the people want, but would be giving the residents of these constituencies their constitutional rights.
The resolution calls for setting up a committee, and the Prime Minister has strongly emphasized that it is to be a fact-finding committee. Naturally some facts will be produced, because where there is smoke there is fire. As we get deeper and deeper into this debate, I for one become more and more convinced that the proposed committee will be permitted only to whitewash the situation. That will be about as far as it will get.
I wish I could be as satisfied in my mind, as the Prime Minister seems to be in his, that the turning of the searchlight of public opinion upon those who have been profiteering-and other members have said there has been-would deter those people. But the turning of the searchlight of public opinion on such persons would have no effect whatsoever on the immense fortunes that have been made. Figures have been quoted, taken from the columns of the Financial Post and other responsible publications, to show that tremendous and abnormal profits have been made, and there is no doubt in my mind that these profits could easily be used in a campaign of propaganda that would deceive almost the angels of heaven if they could read it. We know how these things have been done before.
I am going to take my seat, but, before doing so, I want to remind the Prime Minister once again that the people of the country are asking for the reimposition of price controls and the application of subsidies, and I hope that the government will give due heed to this request. May I, Mr. Speaker, have the privilege of moving the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
